q.s: At 4 weeks of development, where does erythropoiesis occur?
e: Correct. The yolk sac makes blood from 3 to 8 weeks.

q.s: Which organ is the main site of fetal erythropoiesis from 6 weeks until birth?
e: Wrong. A minor site from 10–28 weeks.
Correct. Liver from 6 weeks to birth.

q.s: Over which period does the spleen contribute to fetal erythropoiesis?
When does bone marrow begin erythropoiesis?
e: Correct. Bone marrow from 18 weeks into adult life.

q.s: Which mnemonic gives the order of fetal erythropoietic sites?
e: Correct. Yolk sac, Liver, Spleen, Bone marrow.

q.s: Which globin chains make up embryonic hemoglobins?
What is the chain composition of fetal hemoglobin?
What is the chain composition of HbA2?
Why does HbF have a higher affinity for oxygen than HbA?
e: Correct. Less 2,3-BPG binding raises O2 affinity.

q.s: What is the physiologic advantage of HbF's higher oxygen affinity?
o: Faster delivery to fetal tissues at high Po2
Allows the fetus to take O2 from maternal hemoglobin across the placenta
e: Wrong. A clinical use, not the physiologic reason.

q.s: Which mnemonic describes the switch from fetal to adult hemoglobin?
Which globin chain is produced continuously from fetal life through adulthood?
e: Correct. Alpha is always present after the embryonic period.

q.s: A newborn has mostly HbF at birth. Around what age does β-chain production largely replace γ-chain production?
o: Within the first several months after birth
e: Correct. γ falls and β rises over the first months of life.

q.s: Why do infants with β-thalassemia major usually appear well at birth?
o: Maternal hemoglobin supports them for years
They rely on HbF (α2γ2), which needs no β chains
e: Correct. Symptoms start as γ declines in the first months.

q.s: Which adult hemoglobin is present in small amounts?
e: Correct. α2δ2, a minor adult hemoglobin.

q.s: Between which sites does the transition of erythropoiesis occur around birth?
e: Correct. The liver stops at birth, and the marrow takes over.

q.s: Which hemoglobin is the main form in a fetus at 30 weeks?
Where are the embryonic globins ζ and ε made?
Raising HbF levels helps patients with sickle cell disease. Which property of HbF explains this?
o: Its γ chains do not polymerize with HbS
e: Correct. HbF lacks β chains (hydroxyurea raises HbF).

q.s: Which organ does NOT contribute to fetal erythropoiesis?
e: Correct. Not listed as a site.

rounds.t: Blood groups and hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: A patient with type A blood has which antibodies in plasma?
Which blood type is the universal RBC recipient?
e: Correct. No anti-A, anti-B or anti-D.

q.s: A patient with type O blood can receive RBCs from which donor type?
Which antibody class are the naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B antibodies in a type A or B person?
e: Correct. Type A and B persons make IgM; type O makes IgG and IgM.
Wrong. Type O people also make IgG.

q.s: Why can ABO hemolytic disease occur in a firstborn baby of a type O mother?
o: Type O mothers have preexisting anti-A/anti-B IgG that crosses the placenta
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: Which RBC types can a type AB person donate to?
e: Wrong. They have anti-B and anti-A.
Wrong. Type O is the universal donor.

q.s: An Rh-negative person receives antibodies against which antigen after sensitization?
e: Correct. Rh is the D antigen; anti-D IgG forms after exposure.

q.s: A 30-year-old Rh-negative woman gives birth to her second Rh-positive child. The baby has hydrops fetalis. She received no prenatal care in either pregnancy. Which mechanism caused this?
o: Maternal anti-D IgG formed after the first pregnancy crossed the placenta
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: When are Rh-negative mothers most often exposed to fetal blood in a first pregnancy?
e: Correct. Fetal blood enters maternal circulation, often at delivery.
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: How does anti-D IgG given to an Rh-negative mother prevent hemolytic disease?
o: It clears fetal Rh-positive cells and prevents the mother forming her own anti-D
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: When is anti-D IgG routinely given to Rh-negative pregnant patients?
o: Only if the baby is type O
e: Correct. Also after ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage, trauma or antepartum hemorrhage if the fetus is Rh-positive.
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: Which presentation is typical of ABO hemolytic disease?
o: Mild jaundice within 24 hours of birth
Severe disease only in third pregnancies
e: Correct. ABO disease is usually milder.
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: Which maternal–fetal combination causes ABO hemolytic disease?
o: Type O mother, type A or B fetus
Type AB mother, type A fetus
Type A mother, type O fetus
Type B mother, type B fetus
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: Which treatment is used for a jaundiced neonate with hemolytic disease?
e: Wrong. Given to the mother for prevention.
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: Which minor blood group antigen can cause severe hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn?
e: Correct. Minor incompatibilities can cause disease.
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: A type O-negative person can donate RBCs to which recipients?
e: Wrong. They can receive only O-negative.

q.s: A type B, Rh-positive patient needs blood urgently. Which RBC units are compatible?
o: B or O, Rh positive or negative
e: Wrong. Compatible but not the only option.

q.s: What antigens are on type O red cells?
Which finding is typical of Rh hemolytic disease rather than ABO disease?
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn

q.s: Which event in an Rh-negative pregnant patient with an Rh-positive fetus calls for anti-D IgG?
o: A normal prenatal visit at 8 weeks without bleeding
e: Correct. Also ectopic pregnancy, miscarriage and antepartum hemorrhage.
q.k: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn
